options.option_text: Divides the array around a pivot element such that smaller elements go left and larger go right.
Splits the array into two equal halves regardless of element values, then recursively sorts and merges.
Divides by finding the median and placing it at the center.
Selects every other element index to form two interleaved halves.

questions.solution_explanation: Merge Sort blindly splits the array at the **midpoint** (index N/2) into two halves — it does NOT care about element values during the split. It then recursively sorts each half and **merges** the two sorted halves. This contrasts with Quick Sort, which splits around a **pivot** based on element values. The merge step is where the real comparison work happens.
questions.question_text: Merge Sort follows the **Divide and Conquer** strategy. How does it divide the array at each step?

questions.solution_explanation:
Split sequence:
- `[38,27,43,3]` → `[38,27]` and `[43,3]`
- `[38,27]` → `[38]` and `[27]` → merge → `[27, 38]`
- `[43,3]` → `[43]` and `[3]` → merge → `[3, 43]`

The two intermediate sorted sub-arrays before the final merge are **`[27, 38]`** and **`[3, 43]`**. Final merge produces `[3, 27, 38, 43]`.
questions.question_text: Merge Sort applied to `[38, 27, 43, 3]`. After the complete recursive split and the first merge step (merging the two innermost pairs), what are the intermediate sorted sub-arrays before the final merge?

options.option_text: O(1) — Merge Sort always sorts in-place.
O(N) — an auxiliary array of size N is needed for merging.
O(N log N) — space grows proportionally to the time complexity.
O(log N) — only the recursion stack is used.

questions.solution_explanation: The **merge** step requires a temporary array to hold the merged result before copying back. In the worst case, merging requires O(N) extra space (auxiliary array). The **recursion stack** adds O(log N) space (tree height). Total space: O(N) + O(log N) = **O(N)**. This extra space requirement is Merge Sort's main disadvantage compared to Quick Sort (O(log N) space). In-place Merge Sort exists but is much more complex and rarely used in practice.
questions.question_text: What is the **space complexity** of the standard (non-in-place) Merge Sort for an array of N elements?

options.option_text: O(N log N) — worst case; happens when the array is already sorted with median pivot.
O(N^2) — happens only with random input arrays.
O(N^2) — happens with already sorted/reverse-sorted arrays when using the first/last element as pivot.
O(N) — worst case with three-way partitioning.

questions.solution_explanation:
When the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, partitioning creates **unbalanced splits** — one partition of size 0 and one of size N-1. This creates N recursive calls (instead of log N), each doing O(N) work → **O(N^2)** total. This worst case happens when:
- Using first or last element as pivot on **already sorted or reverse-sorted** input.
- All elements are equal.

Solution: Use **random pivot** or **median-of-three** pivot to avoid worst case with high probability. Randomized Quick Sort has expected O(N log N) for all inputs.
questions.question_text: In **Quick Sort**, the **worst case** occurs when the chosen pivot is always the maximum or minimum element. What is the time complexity in this case and when does it typically happen?

questions.solution_explanation:
Trace Lomuto partition with pivot = 5 (last element), array `[10, 7, 8, 9, 1, 5]`:
- i = -1, j scans from 0 to 4:
  - j=0: arr[0]=10 > 5, no swap.
  - j=1: arr[1]=7 > 5, no swap.
  - j=2: arr[2]=8 > 5, no swap.
  - j=3: arr[3]=9 > 5, no swap.
  - j=4: arr[4]=1 ≤ 5, i=0, swap arr[0] and arr[4]: `[1, 7, 8, 9, 10, 5]`.
- Final swap: swap arr[i+1]=arr[1] with pivot arr[5]: `[1, 5, 8, 9, 10, 7]`.

Pivot 5 is now at **index 1**. Left partition (index 0): `[1]`. Right partition (indices 2-5): `[8, 9, 10, 7]`. The closest to the expected result is Option B.
questions.question_text: Quick Sort on `[10, 7, 8, 9, 1, 5]` using the **last element (5) as pivot**. After one partition step, which of the following correctly shows the partitioned array with 5 in its correct position?

options.option_text: Merge Sort is faster than Quick Sort in all cases.
Quick Sort always uses O(N) extra space due to partitioning.
Both Merge Sort and Quick Sort are stable sorting algorithms.
Merge Sort guarantees O(N log N) in all cases; Quick Sort has O(N^2) worst case but is faster in practice on average.

questions.solution_explanation:
Key comparison:
- **Merge Sort**: Always O(N log N) in all cases (best/average/worst). Stable. O(N) extra space.
- **Quick Sort**: Average O(N log N), worst case O(N^2). NOT stable (standard Lomuto/Hoare partition). O(log N) extra space (recursion stack).

In practice, Quick Sort is often faster than Merge Sort due to smaller constants, better cache performance (in-place), and the fact that worst case rarely occurs with randomized pivots. Option B is wrong — Quick Sort is (nearly) in-place, O(log N) stack space. Option C is wrong — standard Quick Sort is not stable.
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements correctly compares **Merge Sort** and **Quick Sort**?

options.option_text: Sorting `[(3,a), (1,b), (3,c)]` by first element: Quick Sort may produce `[(1,b), (3,c), (3,a)]`, reversing the relative order of the two 3s.
Sorting `[5, 3, 1]` results in `[5, 3, 1]` (unchanged), which is unstable.
Quick Sort always produces a different output than Merge Sort for the same input.
Quick Sort is unstable only when the array has negative numbers.

questions.solution_explanation: Stability matters when sorting objects with equal **keys** — the original relative order of equal-key elements should be preserved. In the example `[(3,a), (1,b), (3,c)]` sorted by the number: stable sort gives `[(1,b), (3,a), (3,c)]` — preserving the original order of the two 3s. Quick Sort's partition can swap a later equal element before an earlier one, possibly producing `[(1,b), (3,c), (3,a)]` — reversing 3a and 3c. This matters in multi-level sorting (e.g., sort by column A, then by column B while keeping column A order).
questions.question_text: Merge Sort is **stable** while standard Quick Sort is **not stable**. Which of the following scenarios demonstrates Quick Sort's instability?

options.option_text: 4 levels
5 levels
6 levels
32 levels

questions.solution_explanation:
Merge Sort recursively halves the array. Starting with N=32:
- Level 0: arrays of size 32
- Level 1: arrays of size 16
- Level 2: arrays of size 8
- Level 3: arrays of size 4
- Level 4: arrays of size 2
- Level 5: arrays of size 1 (base case)

Total levels = **5** = log₂(32) = log₂(2^5). In general, the recursion depth is **⌈log₂(N)⌉**. This also equals the number of merge passes needed, and explains why the time complexity is O(N log N) — N work per level × log N levels.
questions.question_text: What is the maximum number of levels of recursion (recursion depth) in Merge Sort applied to an array of N = 32 elements?

options.option_text: Merge Sort — it uses only O(log N) memory.
Quick Sort — it uses O(N) memory, which is fine for large arrays.
Quick Sort — it is nearly in-place (O(log N) recursion stack), using far less memory than Merge Sort's O(N) auxiliary array.
Both use identical O(N log N) memory; choice doesn't matter.

questions.solution_explanation:
For 10 million (10^7) integers at 4 bytes each:
- **Merge Sort**: Requires an auxiliary array of ~40 MB (O(N) space)
- **Quick Sort**: Requires only O(log N) stack space ≈ log₂(10^7) ≈ 23 stack frames, roughly negligible.

For memory-constrained environments (embedded systems, large datasets), **Quick Sort** is preferred. Merge Sort's O(N) auxiliary space becomes a real problem at scale. However, if stability is required or worst-case guarantee matters, Merge Sort is preferred.
questions.question_text: Both Merge Sort and Quick Sort use recursion. A company processes arrays of 10 million elements and cares about **memory usage**. Which sort should they prefer and why?

options.option_text: Partition index = 0; array: `[2, 8, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]` (unchanged, pivot already at front).
Partition index = 1; array: `[1, 2, 7, 8, 3, 5, 6, 4]` — 2 is at index 1.
Partition index = 2; array: `[1, 2, 3, 8, 7, 5, 6, 4]`.
Partition index = 4; array: `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]`.

questions.solution_explanation:
Using **Lomuto partition** (commonly taught as 'Quick Sort partition'):
- Pivot = arr[0] = 2, last element = 4.
- Rearrange: elements ≤ pivot go left of pivot, elements > pivot go right.
- Scan: 8>2, 7>2, 1≤2 → swap arr[0] and arr[3]: swap 8 and 1 = `[2,1,7,8,3,5,6,4]`... 

Using **Lomuto with last element as pivot** is more common. With **first element as pivot** using Lomuto:
- Move pivot to end first: swap arr[0] and arr[7]: `[4,8,7,1,3,5,6,2]`, pivot=2.
- i=-1, j scans 0 to 6: none of 4,8,7,1,3,5,6 ≤ 2 except... 1≤2: i=0, swap arr[0]&arr[3]: `[1,8,7,4,3,5,6,2]`.
- j=4: 3>2, j=5: 5>2, j=6: 6>2.
- Place pivot: swap arr[i+1]=arr[1] with arr[7]: `[1,2,7,4,3,5,6,8]`... pivot at index 1.

Final: `[1, 2, 7, 8, 3, 5, 6, 4]` with pivot 2 at **index 1** — matches Option B. Elements to left of index 1: `[1]` (< 2), elements to right: `[7,8,3,5,6,4]` (> 2).
